readerTitle: Who pays for the free newspaper?
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Metro, Financial Times) + 실제 관찰 (의료, 아동용품, 사내 소프트웨어) + 가상 사례 (학원, 구내식당)
insight: 사용자와 지불자가 다르면, 제품은 지불자 쪽으로 휘어진다.
misconception: "공짜면 당신이 상품이다"로 모든 걸 설명할 수 있다.

sources.text: Metro International, company history (launch in Stockholm, 1995)
Financial Times / Nikkei, annual reports and public statements on subscription revenue

factChecks.note: Metro는 1995년 스톡홀름에서 시작한 무료 통근 신문입니다. 이후 여러 나라에서 발행 구조와 소유가 바뀌었으니, 카드에는 출발 시점의 모델만 적었습니다.
Financial Times의 매출에서 구독 등 콘텐츠 매출이 광고보다 크다는 점은 FT·Nikkei의 공개 자료로 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 비율 숫자를 넣지 않았습니다.
시리얼 박스 캐릭터의 눈높이 배치는 여러 언론에서 보도한 관찰이지만, 원 연구는 표본이 한정적입니다. 카드에는 일반적인 관찰로만 적었습니다.
학원의 첫 판단 문제는 정답이 없는 문제입니다. 선택지마다 사업이 어떻게 달라지는지만 보여줍니다.

cards.title: Who pays for the free newspaper?
body: On a morning train, one commuter reads a free newspaper handed out at the station. Another reads a paper they pay a subscription for.
Same kind of product. Very different businesses.

image.label: Two commuters, two newspapers
image.brief: 아침 지하철. 한 사람은 역에서 받은 얇은 무료 신문을, 다른 사람은 두꺼운 유료 경제지를 읽고 있음. 실제 매체 로고 없음.

cards.title: Who should pay for your tutoring center?
body: You run an after-school tutoring center. Students like it, and now you need to decide who your main paying customer is.
There's no right answer here. Pick one and see what it does to the business.

options.feedback: Students pay for quick help before exams. The service drifts toward last-minute cramming, and most students have little money.
Parents pay for progress they can see. You'll need reports and regular check-ins. Students may feel watched.
Schools pay for results across a whole class. Expect slow decisions, contracts and reporting. Individual students' wishes may come last.

choice.afterReveal: Every choice reshapes the business. **Whoever pays shapes what gets built.**

cards.title: A free commuter paper vs a paid business paper
body: **Metro**, the free commuter newspaper that started in Stockholm in 1995, was paid for by advertisers. It was built for a short ride: brief articles, handed out where commuters gather. Reaching many commuters is what its advertisers were buying.
The **Financial Times** earns most of its money from readers who subscribe. It's built around in-depth reporting readers can't easily get elsewhere, because that's what its paying customers buy.
Both models make sense. Each one follows its money.

cards.title: The user and the payer
body: The **user** is who uses the product. The **payer** is who pays for it. Sometimes they're the same person. Often they aren't.

When they differ, the product tends to serve the payer first. That explains a lot: why some workplace software is clunky (managers buy it, employees use it), and why cereal boxes speak to kids with cartoons and to parents with health claims.

image.label: Two figures: one holds the product, one holds the wallet
image.brief: 두 사람 일러스트. 왼쪽 사람은 신문(제품)을 들고 있고, 오른쪽 사람은 지갑을 들고 있음. 신문에서 나온 화살표가 지갑을 든 사람 쪽으로 기울어 있음.

cards.title: Users and payers are split everywhere.
list: **Healthcare:** the patient receives care, a doctor often chooses it, and an insurer or government often pays.
**Children's products:** children use them, parents pay.
**Staff canteens and uniforms:** employees use them, the employer pays.
**Free TV and many websites:** viewers watch, advertisers pay.
cards.softwareNote: Employees use workplace tools that IT or finance buys. Consumers use free apps paid for by advertisers or by the few users who upgrade. Before you write your pricing page, decide whose problem it's written for.

cards.title: "If it's free, you're the product" is too simple.
body: Ad-funded businesses still need their audience to stay, so the audience's experience matters to the payer too.
Paying doesn't guarantee alignment either. A gym with paying members can still make cancelling hard.
The better question: **what does the payer reward, and does that help or hurt the user?**

cards.title: Your staff canteen contract is up for renewal.
body: Your catering company runs a staff canteen. Employees eat for free, and their employer pays you per employee. What do you need to show the employer?

options.text: Lots of employees eat there every day
options.feedback: Useful evidence, but how many people eat isn't exactly what the employer is buying.

options.text: That the canteen helps the company, such as staff satisfaction or retention, with numbers to back it
options.feedback: That's what the payer pays for. Meals are the means. Outcomes the employer cares about are the goal.

options.text: A bigger menu than any other caterer
options.feedback: Variety matters to the people eating. The payer wants results for the company.

cards.title: Follow the money to understand the business.
body: For any business, ask two questions: who uses it, and who pays? Where the answers differ, expect the business to lean toward the payer.
**Try it today:** pick a product or service you use every week. Who pays for it? What would change if you were the one paying?
